gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what it costs to keep each NAS running all day and night, which a Nextcloud server must do: at the US average home rate of 18.16¢/kWh (August 2026), the makers' own power figures come to about $60 a year for the Synology DS925+, $64 for the QNAP TS-464 and $27 for the Synology DS225+ with the drives awake, versus $20, $34 and $10 with the drives asleep.
standout_why: I opened three pages. racksandwatts.com's 2026 homelab guide, cited in two chats, lists only installed and maximum RAM. It has no watts, no running cost and no dollar prices, and never mentions Nextcloud. esp32.co.uk's best 4-bay NAS for Docker guide, cited once, has no power figures and no prices, and names Nextcloud only in passing. Our own dealectric page has full-unit prices but no watts and no running cost. The cited QNAP spec page lists the TS-464's watts but never turns them into a cost or compares them with other models.
decides: This confirms the shortlist rather than changing it. The QNAP TS-464 costs the most to run in the makers' own figures: 40.5 W typical against 37.9 W for the DS925+ while drives are being accessed (about $4 more a year), and 21.6 W against 12.3 W with drives asleep (about $15 more a year). So its $639 price edge over the DS925+ ($829.99 at Micro Center in ChatGPT's answer) shrinks a little over 5 years. The DS225+ is by far the cheapest to run, about $27 a year, but tops out at 6 GB of RAM, short of the 16 GB ChatGPT recommends. Nextcloud's background jobs every 5 minutes tend to keep the hard drives from sleeping unless its data sits on SSD, so the drives-awake figure is the realistic one. That makes 'put the database on NVMe' a running-cost point as well as a speed point. For the DXP4800 Plus I could only source a reviewer's idle reading (KitGuru, 24.25 W, about $39 a year), which isn't comparable with the maker figures.
